alternatives: For pain: acetaminophen up to 2 g per day rather than opioids or NSAIDs.
For nausea: ondansetron rather than promethazine or other sedating antiemetics.
For osteoporosis: a non-constipating regimen, or calcium carbonate only with the lactulose titrated to 2-3 soft stools a day.
contraindications: Benzodiazepines, opioids and sedating antihistamines or antiemetics in overt hepatic encephalopathy: they deepen and prolong the encephalopathy.
interactions: Calcium carbonate 1000 mg twice daily is constipating and adds to the constipation that precipitated this episode.

Azathioprine with prednisone: immunosuppression raises the risk of infection, which can be occult in cirrhosis; monitor the blood count (azathioprine myelotoxicity) beside the hypersplenic thrombocytopenia.
Prednisone 5 mg daily for years: do not stop abruptly (adrenal suppression); consider stress-dose corticosteroid if she becomes septic or hypotensive.

Furosemide and spironolactone with poor oral intake in overt hepatic encephalopathy: dehydration and electrolyte shifts can worsen the encephalopathy; holding them during the acute episode is advised.
Lactulose and rifaximin: no clinically relevant interaction with the current medicines.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not give benzodiazepines or other sedatives for agitation or sleep: they precipitate and prolong hepatic encephalopathy; manage agitation with reorientation, a safe environment and treatment of the precipitant (EASL 2022).
Do not prescribe opioids, which worsen HE; for pain use acetaminophen up to 2 g per day.
Do not order serial ammonia levels to guide lactulose titration; response is judged clinically (ACG 2026 recommendation 5).
required_recommendations: Identify and treat the precipitants: six days of constipation (last stool four days ago) and four to five days without lactulose, with calcium carbonate as a constipating contributor.

Lactulose 25 mL every 1-2 hours until at least two soft bowel movements, then titrated to 2-3 soft bowel movements per day (ACG 2026 recommendation 10; EASL 2022); avoid over-titration, which causes dehydration, hypokalemia and kidney injury.

If she cannot swallow safely, give lactulose by nasogastric tube or as a retention enema, and monitor airway and consciousness with escalation to a high-dependency or intensive care setting if the GCS falls.
Continue rifaximin 550 mg twice daily with lactulose for this recurrent overt episode (ACG 2026; EASL 2022).

Hold furosemide and spironolactone during the overt episode with poor oral intake, and restart them at the 100:40 ratio with sodium, potassium and creatinine monitoring once she is eating and alert (EASL 2018).
Continue azathioprine and prednisone without abrupt steroid withdrawal (adrenal suppression), with stress-dose corticosteroid if she becomes septic, and monitor the blood count.

Before discharge: a lactulose refill and adherence plan titrated to 2-3 soft stools a day, review of the calcium carbonate, and supervision at home because she lives alone after a second overt episode.
Refer for liver transplant assessment: decompensated cirrhosis with ascites and recurrent overt HE, MELD-Na 16 (EASL 2018).

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion for hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, or endocarditis; echocardiography is not part of the acute HE workup.
Amyloid PET has no role in acute HE workup; the AMS is attributable to reversible metabolic encephalopathy, not Alzheimer pathology.
FDG-PET has no role in acute HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the clinical question, not paraneoplastic or neurodegenerative disease.
Formal neuropsychological testing cannot be validly performed during overt HE; indicated only for evaluation of minimal/covert HE after the acute episode resolves.

accepted: Hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven grade III), autoimmune hepatitis cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C, MELD-Na 16), precipitated by constipation and lactulose non-adherence

differential.key_features: Excluded: ascitic PMN 44 cells/mm3, Gram stain negative, culture no growth.
Immunosuppressed, but afebrile, WBC 5.2, CRP 2 mg/L, lactate 1.4 mmol/L, and blood and urine cultures without growth.
Platelets 102 and INR 1.5 in a woman living alone; CT shows no hemorrhage.
Azathioprine does not cause encephalopathy at standard doses, and the dose has been stable for years.

key_clinical_evidence: Child-Pugh C (10: bilirubin 2.8 2, albumin 2.9 2, INR 1.5 1, small ascites 2, HE grade 3 3); MELD-Na 16 (creatinine 0.8, bilirubin 2.8, INR 1.5, sodium 136)

HE is a clinical diagnosis: lethargy, disorientation to time and place, asterixis and GCS 12 in known cirrhosis with a clear precipitant, after other causes of altered mental status are excluded (ACG 2026; EASL 2022).

An elevated ammonia neither grades nor confirms hepatic encephalopathy and repeat levels are not used to guide treatment; a normal ammonia in a confused patient with cirrhosis should prompt a search for another cause (ACG 2026 recommendation 5 and key concept 14; EASL 2022).
Normal electrolytes, glucose and renal function, no inflammatory response, negative cultures and a normal ascitic PMN count leave constipation and lactulose non-adherence as the precipitants.
Lactulose non-adherence is one of the most common modifiable HE precipitants: patients stop it when they feel well, so discharge needs a refill and titration plan.
Long-term azathioprine and prednisone make infection more likely and less visible, which is why the paracentesis and the infection screen matter even without fever.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Ammonia neither grades nor confirms hepatic encephalopathy (ACG 2026 recommendation 5 and key concept 14). The diagnosis rests on clinical grounds: GCS 12, bilateral asterixis, disorientation and a clear precipitant in known cirrhosis.

patient.history_present_illness:
Mrs. E. is a 67-year-old woman with autoimmune hepatitis cirrhosis who was brought to the emergency department by her son after three days of worsening confusion and lethargy. Her son had called to check on her three days ago and noted she seemed unusually slow and repetitive on the phone. When he visited yesterday, he found her sleeping at midday, disoriented about the day of the week, and unable to recall a conversation from two hours earlier. She called her cat by a wrong name and left the front door unlocked overnight. This morning he could not rouse her to full alertness and brought her in.

On further history, the son reports that his mother had been complaining of constipation for approximately six days, attributing it to reduced dietary fiber and decreased fluid intake over the prior week because of poor appetite. She had not taken her lactulose doses for the past four to five days because she had run out and had not refilled the prescription; she had been feeling well recently and thought she could skip it temporarily. She had continued her rifaximin regularly. Her last bowel movement was four days ago. She denied dark stools, hematemesis, abdominal pain, or fever. No recent sick contacts, travel, or new medications. No falls or head trauma. There is no history of alcohol or recreational substance use.

Her prior HE episode eight months ago had resolved promptly with lactulose restart within 48 hours. Her hepatologist had emphasized strict lactulose adherence at that visit, but the patient had felt well and had a permissive attitude toward medication adherence. Review of systems is otherwise unremarkable except for mild nausea over the past week. She has no urinary symptoms.
